name: Joseph P. Kennedy Sr.
role: First SEC chairman (1934-35), first Maritime Commission chairman (1937-38), U.S. ambassador to Britain (1938-40)
summary: A businessman and Roosevelt ally who accepted New Deal financial regulation as protecting investors and legitimate business, while insisting honest enterprise had nothing to fear. In foreign affairs he opposed U.S. entry into the Second World War while favouring aid to Britain, objected to Lend-Lease as an executive power grab, and after 1947 argued against Cold War commitments, urging withdrawal from Korea and Asia and a focus on the domestic economy.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Inferred: he called the complaint that there was 'too much Government in business' a baseless lament and described regulation as necessary to restrain 'the power of the strong over the weak', which points away from trusting free markets alone; he never addressed the comparison directly.

regulate-corporations.rationale: As SEC chairman he said the regulation of the investment market 'must be apparent to all right-thinking people', that 'we cannot turn back', and that for dishonest promoters the rules 'can't be too strict'; he backed disclosure and supervision of corporations, while stressing honest business had nothing to fear.

strong-leader.rationale: Mixed: in January 1941 he said he was 'a great believer in centralized responsibility', yet opposed the Lend-Lease bill as a surrender of Congress's authority to the executive.

state-harmful.rationale: Inferred: he defended an expanding role for government agencies and called it unmanly to blame government for business's own lack of courage, which is incompatible with the state being unnecessary and harmful.

empower-police-military.rationale: Mixed over time: in 1941 he urged going 'all out' for rearmament and arming 'to the teeth', but in 1947-50 he opposed Cold War military budgets on economic grounds.

nation-first.rationale: In 1941 he said the test of any proposal should be 'what is best for the United States of America'; in 1950 he urged leaving Asian commitments the U.S. would not defend for its own sake.

state-directs-investment.rationale: His Maritime Commission administered federal subsidies to rebuild the merchant fleet and replaced old mail contracts with direct subsidies; he carried out a statutory program rather than stating a general view, so this is low.

democracy-best.rationale: He said 'we want to preserve our democracy' and did not want a dictatorship of the right or left (1941); he also said in 1940 that democracy was finished in England, and nothing addresses voters choosing badly, so low.

military-superiority.rationale: Mixed: in 1941 he urged building strength to be secure against any power or group of powers, but after 1947 he argued Cold War military spending would harm the economy and that the U.S. need not hold positions abroad.

class-collaboration.rationale: The 1937 Maritime Commission report, issued under his chairmanship, said no lasting cure for maritime labor strife would come until unions and ship operators reached a 'more cooperative working arrangement'.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Inferred: as SEC and Maritime Commission chairman he administered market supervision, wage floors and subsidies, and defended such functions as legitimate, beyond defence, justice and property protection.

separated-powers.rationale: In January 1941 he objected that the Lend-Lease bill would vest in the executive powers 'unheard of in our history' and amount to a surrender of the authority and responsibility of Congress.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Contested and narrow: the Commission he chaired condemned sit-down and quickie strikes on ships and recommended remedial legislation after the Algic incident, and a union biography reports he pushed to outlaw maritime strikes; this concerns seamen only and secret ballots are not mentioned.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: In December 1950 he called for getting out of Korea and every point in Asia not needed for U.S. defence, then applying 'the same principle in Europe', including ending support for Chiang and the French in Indochina (as reported by Nasaw via The Nation).

collective-defense.rationale: Inferred: in 1950 he urged applying the withdrawal principle to Europe and rejected fighting Communism abroad; in 1941 he left hemisphere defence to other countries' self-interest.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Inferred: he argued in 1934-35 that regulation would restore confidence and that business could recover under the new securities laws ('We cannot turn back'), implying capitalism could be reformed rather than collapse; no direct statement on collapse theory.

defeat-communism.rationale: In 1947 he argued the U.S. should 'permit communism outside the Soviet Union to have its trial' and in 1950 that negotiating with the Soviets was not weakness; he judged Communism harmful but not to be fought abroad.

social-market-economy.rationale: Inferred: he was a strong supporter of the New Deal and defended regulation as protecting both investors and honest business, which fits a market economy with public protections; he did not frame it in these terms.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: In 1950 he held that Communist rule abroad was not a threat to U.S. security and proposed withdrawing from Asia and Europe; earlier he supported neutrality after 1939 and urged staying out of the European war.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: In January 1941 he said 'Unless we are attacked, the American people do not have to go to war', though he added the U.S. would fight if vital interests were at stake.

arms-reduction.rationale: Inferred: in 1947 and 1950 he argued proposed Cold War military budgets would 'seriously affect the economic well-being of our country' and urged withdrawal from Korea and elsewhere in Asia, which points to lower armaments; he did not state a general level.

notes: Full texts of the 1936 book I'm for Roosevelt, the December 1950 University of Virginia speech and the 1941 Lend-Lease testimony were not obtainable, so the 1950 positions rest on quotations reported by The Nation from Nasaw. Reported private remarks about Jews are secondhand and were left null. Support for Joseph McCarthy is a record of donations, not stated views on any statement.
